## Object

$$T(x) = \begin{cases} 1/q & x = p/q,\ \gcd(p,q)=1,\ q>0\\ 0 & x \notin \mathbb{Q}.\end{cases}$$

## Why it works

Fix irrational $x_0$ and $\varepsilon > 0$. Only finitely many rationals in
$(x_0-1, x_0+1)$ have denominator $\le 1/\varepsilon$; a neighborhood of $x_0$ avoiding
them gives $T < \varepsilon$ throughout — continuity at $x_0$. At rational $x_0$,
$T(x_0) > 0$ but irrationals approach with value $0$. For integrability: given
$\varepsilon$, the finitely many points with $T \ge \varepsilon$ are covered by intervals
of total length $\varepsilon$, so upper sums drop below $2\varepsilon$.

## What it kills

The mental model "continuity points form intervals" and the converse error "dense
discontinuities ⇒ not integrable". Paired with the Dirichlet function it separates
*dense* from *full-measure*.

## Debugging uses

- Test claims of the form "continuity on a dense set implies X": T is continuous on a
  dense set, yet unbounded variation on every interval and monotone on no interval.
- The asymmetry probe: there is no function continuous exactly on the rationals (G_δ
  obstruction). Any argument that "constructs" one must break on the Baire category step.
- Sanity input for adaptive quadrature/mesh-refinement logic: the singular set is dense,
  so refinement heuristics keyed to "isolated bad points" are violated, yet the true
  integral is 0.

## Remarks

$T$ is nowhere differentiable — differentiability fails even at the irrationals
(rational approximations with slowly growing denominators get too close).
hits.counterexample: T(p/q) = 1/q for p/q in lowest terms (T(0)=1), T(x) = 0 for x irrational. T is continuous at every irrational, discontinuous at every rational, and Riemann integrable on [0,1] with integral 0. Its discontinuity set Q is dense but has measure zero.
hits.refutes: (a) A function continuous on a dense set is continuous on an interval, or at least somewhere "nice". (b) A function discontinuous on a dense set cannot be Riemann integrable. (c) If f is continuous at every irrational, some interval is free of discontinuities.

Take k=3, ε=1, U={a1,a2,a3,b1,b2,b3,c1,c2,c3}, m1={a1,a2,a3}, m2={b1,b2,b3}, and fi={a1,b1,ci} for i=1,2,3. Let C={m1,m2,f1,f2,f3}, n=5, M={m1,m2}, and x_fi=1/3, x_mj=0. Then F=F2={f1,f2,f3}. ## What it kills

The flagged claim: **Let \(I=(\mathcal U,\mathcal C)\) be a \(k\)-set-packing instance with \(|\mathcal C|=n\), let \(\varepsilon>0\), and let \(M\subseteq\mathcal C\) be a \(4(1+1/\varepsilon)\log_2 n\)-locally optimal matching (that is, a packing of mutually disjoint sets). Let \(x\) be any feasible solution to the intersecting-family LP, let \(\mathcal F=\{f\in\mathcal C:x_f>0\}\), and let \(\mathcal F_2\) consist of those \(f\in\mathcal F\) that intersect exactly two members of \(M\). Define the auxiliary undirected multigraph \(H\) to have one vertex \(v_m\) for every \(m\in M\) and one edge \(e_f\) for every \(f\in\mathcal F_2\), joining \(v_{m_1}\) and \(v_{m_2}\) when \(m_1,m_2\) are the two members of \(M\) intersected by \(f\); distinct members of \(\mathcal F_2\) may therefore give parallel edges. For every \(X\subseteq V(H)\), let \(\mathcal B_X=\{f\in\mathcal F_2:e_f\in E(H[X])\}\). If \(|E(H[X])|>|X|\), then \(\mathcal B_X\) is an improving set for \(M\): \(\mathcal B_X\) is a packing and, in the intersection graph \(G\) of the packings \(M\) and \(\mathcal B_X\), \(N_G(B_X,M)=N(B_X)\cap M\) and \(\left|(M\cup B_X)\setminus N_G(B_X,M)\right|>|M|\). Equivalently, adding the source sets corresponding to the edges of \(H[X]\) and removing the members of \(M\) that they intersect yields a mutually disjoint solution of larger cardinality.**

> By $\mathcal{U}$ we mean the universe of elements over which the $k$-set system $\mathcal{C} \subseteq 2^{\mathcal{U}}$ has been defined. We write $|\mathcal{U}| = N$ and $|\mathcal{C}| = n$. By $I = (\mathcal{U},\mathcal{C})$ a given instance for $k$-set packing is denoted in which the objective is to find the largest packing.
> 
> Now let $\mathcal{A}$ be some solution to this instance, i.e. a collection of subsets in $\mathcal{C}$ that are mutually disjoint.
> 
> \begin{defn}
> \textbf{(Intersection graph)} Let an instance $I$ for the $k$-set packing problem be given and let $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$ be two packings. The intersection graph of $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$ is the induced subgraph of their vertices in the conflict graph of $I$.
> \end{defn}
> 
> The bipartite intersection graph of $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$ thus contains a vertex for every set in $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$ and two vertices
> are adjacent
> if and only if
> the subsets in the set packing instance are in conflict. Throughout this thesis calligraphic letters $\mathcal{A}$ will be used to denote collections of subsets and normal letters $A$ to denote the set of vertices corresponding to $\mathcal{A}$ in the conflict or intersection graph. Denote $N_G(B,A) = N(B) \cap A$, the neighbours of $B$ in $A$ in their intersection graph $G$. Sometimes for brevity we just write $N(G,A)$ if the graph $G$ is clear from the context. We can now succinctly define an improving set.
> 
> \begin{defn}
> [...]

Context of the original problem:

> Title: On local search and LP and SDP relaxations for k-Set Packing

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

## Why it works

M is globally maximum: every fi conflicts with both m1 and m2, and the fi are pairwise conflicting, so every packing outside M has size at most 1; hence M is t-locally optimal for t=8 log2(5), indeed for every t. The LP vector is feasible: every pairwise-intersecting family of positive-weight sets contains at most f1,f2,f3, whose total weight is 1 (element constraints, if included, also hold). Thus every hypothesis holds, but the asserted conclusion that B_X is a packing—and hence a feasible improving set—is false.

> All supplied finite hypotheses hold, but B_X={f1,f2,f3} is not a packing: f1 and f2 intersect in {a1,b1}. Thus the asserted implication is false, despite its displayed cardinality being 3>2.

> Actual result: |E(H[X])|=3>|X|=2, but B_X is not a packing; its members share a1 and b1. The formal displayed residual cardinality is 3, which does not establish a feasible replacement.
> Negative control: After replacing f2,f3 by {a2,b2,c2},{a3,b3,c3}, the three source sets are a packing and give residual size 3; this is a size-3 improvement, so M is not locally optimal.

The flagged claim: **The DP recurrence S(1:n,1:n) = max over the four corner choices (corner element + optimal sum of the opposite (n-1)x(n-1) contiguous square sub-array) computes the maximum assignment sum (one element per row and per column).**

The flawed step reads, verbatim from the source:

> That is, the optimal sum for a square array of size `n` can be determined by separately computing the optimal sum for each of the four sub-arrays of size `n-1`, and then maximising the sum of the sub-array and the element that was "left out".

> Maximise sum of "non-overlapping" numbers in square array - help with proof

The claim asserts the equality S(1:n,1:n) = max assignment sum for every square array, so a single finite integer array refutes it. $$f_n = n\,\chi_{(0,1/n)}: \qquad f_n(x) \to 0 \ \forall x, \qquad \int_0^1 f_n = 1 \not\to 0.$$

The mass 1 concentrates into a shrinking set; in the limit it is carried by "width zero
times height infinity". As distributions, $f_n \to \delta_0$ — the lost mass is exactly
the Dirac point mass.

## What it kills

Interchanging $\lim$ and $\int$ by default. Note the convergence here is even monotone
after the peak passes each fixed x, a.e., and on a probability space — none of that
suffices without domination or uniform integrability.

## Debugging uses

- The universal probe for limit–integral interchanges, differentiation under the
  integral sign, and term-by-term integration of series. If a proof's envelope
  candidate fails on the moving bump, the proof has a gap.
- Probability: X_n = n with prob. 1/n, else 0 — X_n → 0 a.s. but E[X_n] = 1. Kills
  "a.s. convergence implies convergence of expectations"; the reason uniform
  integrability appears in martingale convergence and why bounded loss/clipping
  assumptions appear in learning-theory proofs.
- Numerics: quadrature on a fixed mesh eventually misses the bump entirely and reports
  0 — concentration defeats fixed sampling; adaptive schemes need the width scale.

## Remarks

The three canonical failure modes of ∫lim = lim∫ are: concentration (this bump),
escape to horizontal infinity (χ_(n,n+1)), escape to vertical infinity on a null set.
Uniform integrability + tightness rules out all three (and is essentially necessary).

## Object

$$f_n = n\,\chi_{(0,1/n)}: \qquad f_n(x) \to 0 \ \forall x, \qquad \int_0^1 f_n = 1 \not\to 0.$$

The mass 1 concentrates into a shrinking set; in the limit it is carried by "width zero
times height infinity". As distributions, $f_n \to \delta_0$ — the lost mass is exactly
the Dirac point mass.

## What it kills

Interchanging $\lim$ and $\int$ by default. Note the convergence here is even monotone
after the peak passes each fixed x, a.e., and on a probability space — none of that
suffices without domination or uniform integrability.

## Debugging uses

- The universal probe for limit–integral interchanges, differentiation under the
  integral sign, and term-by-term integration of series. If a proof's envelope
  candidate fails on the moving bump, the proof has a gap.
- Probability: X_n = n with prob. 1/n, else 0 — X_n → 0 a.s. but E[X_n] = 1. Kills
  "a.s. convergence implies convergence of expectations"; the reason uniform
  integrability appears in martingale convergence and why bounded loss/clipping
  assumptions appear in learning-theory proofs.
- Numerics: quadrature on a fixed mesh eventually misses the bump entirely and reports
  0 — concentration defeats fixed sampling; adaptive schemes need the width scale.

## Remarks

The three canonical failure modes of ∫lim = lim∫ are: concentration (this bump),
escape to horizontal infinity (χ_(n,n+1)), escape to vertical infinity on a null set.
Uniform integrability + tightness rules out all three (and is essentially necessary).

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

## Why it works

The sentence asserts a universally quantified, finitely checkable implication: for all finite S of positive integers with gcd(S)=1, all n, if there exists e in S with e <= n - m (m = Frobenius number of S) then the distance graph G_n(S) on n vertices is connected. A single (n, S) pair refutes it.

The script computes m exactly by dynamic-programming reachability over a range extended past the Frobenius number, with an assertion certifying that min(S) consecutive top entries are representable (so everything beyond is representable); connectivity is computed by exact integer union-find. Pure Python ints throughout, no floats in any decision, no randomness.

Result: 343 distinct violating pairs. The extremal witness S={2,3}, n=3 satisfies the hypothesis with e = 2 = n - m yet has c = 2. The correct sufficient condition is e + m <= n - 1, i.e. e <= n - m - 1: to walk from a vertex to a neighbouring residue one needs a displacement of size at most n-1 that decomposes as e plus a representable amount, and at e = n - m the required displacement e + m = n just exceeds the largest difference n-1 available on n vertices. Consistent with that diagnosis, the sweep found ZERO violations of the corrected bound over the entire space, while every violation of the stated bound occurred exactly at equality e = n - m.

CAVEAT (stated honestly, since I was blind to the source): the witness depends on reading G_n(S) as the n-vertex distance graph on {1,...,n}. Under a circulant reading Cay(Z_n, S) the statement would be vacuously true (gcd(S)=1 already forces connectivity), and under an (n+1)-vertex reading {0,...,n} the boundary shifts by one and S={2,3}, n=3 is connected (reported in the script output as c = 1). The flag's stated correction "e <= n - m - 1" matches the n-vertex reading, and the perfect empirical separation (343 failures at e = n-m, 0 failures at e <= n-m-1) is strong internal evidence that this is the intended reading.

## Object

$$f_n = n\,\chi_{(0,1/n)}: \qquad f_n(x) \to 0 \ \forall x, \qquad \int_0^1 f_n = 1 \not\to 0.$$

The mass 1 concentrates into a shrinking set; in the limit it is carried by "width zero
times height infinity". As distributions, $f_n \to \delta_0$ — the lost mass is exactly
the Dirac point mass.

## What it kills

Interchanging $\lim$ and $\int$ by default. Note the convergence here is even monotone
after the peak passes each fixed x, a.e., and on a probability space — none of that
suffices without domination or uniform integrability.

## Debugging uses

- The universal probe for limit–integral interchanges, differentiation under the
  integral sign, and term-by-term integration of series. If a proof's envelope
  candidate fails on the moving bump, the proof has a gap.
- Probability: X_n = n with prob. 1/n, else 0 — X_n → 0 a.s. but E[X_n] = 1. Kills
  "a.s. convergence implies convergence of expectations"; the reason uniform
  integrability appears in martingale convergence and why bounded loss/clipping
  assumptions appear in learning-theory proofs.
- Numerics: quadrature on a fixed mesh eventually misses the bump entirely and reports
  0 — concentration defeats fixed sampling; adaptive schemes need the width scale.

## Remarks

The three canonical failure modes of ∫lim = lim∫ are: concentration (this bump),
escape to horizontal infinity (χ_(n,n+1)), escape to vertical infinity on a null set.
Uniform integrability + tightness rules out all three (and is essentially necessary).

## Object

$$T = \overline{\{(x, \sin(1/x)) : x > 0\}} = S \cup (\{0\}\times[-1,1]).$$

Connectedness: $S$ is a continuous image of $(0,\infty)$, hence connected, and
$S \subseteq T \subseteq \overline S$ forces $T$ connected. Non-path-connectedness: a
path from $(0,0)$ into $S$ would have to traverse infinitely many full oscillations in
finite time; formally, continuity at the boundary segment fails against the sequence
$x_k = 1/(\arcsin y + 2\pi(k+1))$ of preimages of any fixed height $y$.

## What it kills

The identification of the two standard notions of "one piece." Also the stability
error: $S$ is path-connected but $\overline S$ is not — closure preserves
connectedness, not path-connectedness.

## Debugging uses

- Any argument that upgrades connectedness to path-connectedness (or joins two
  points of a connected set by a path "WLOG") must invoke local path-connectedness;
  T is the universal witness that this hypothesis earns its place.
- Mesh/graphics intuition check: T is compact, connected, and yet has no finite-length
  approach to part of itself — algorithms that trace connected components by paths
  (flood fill along curves, marching methods) implicitly assume local path-connectedness.
- The oscillation mechanism is the same one as in `x2-sin-inverse-x`: sin(1/x) is the
  one canonical generator of accumulating-oscillation pathologies, worth knowing in
  both its analytic and topological costumes.

## Why the formalization matters

Fully machine-verified in mathlib: `TopologistsSineCurve.isConnected_T` and
`TopologistsSineCurve.not_isPathConnected_T` (Counterexamples library; from a
UniDistance Switzerland bachelor thesis — an indication of the scale of such a
formalization project).

## References

Also Steen & Seebach, *Counterexamples in Topology* (the closed topologist's sine
curve), and Gelbaum–Olmsted's plane-sets chapter (unverified citation).
